title: Conditional Probability
rights: Original teacher-authored public-safe practice; no secure homework.

items.prompt: A café records 8 app orders, of which 2 are tea. What is P(tea | app)?
items.hint: Given app means the denominator is the eight app orders.
items.solution: Two of the eight app orders are tea, so P(tea|app)=2/8=1/4.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: The same café has 10 tea orders, 2 of which came through the app. What is P(app | tea)?
items.hint: Given tea restricts the sample space to the 10 tea orders.
items.solution: Two of ten tea orders used the app, giving 2/10=1/5.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Two of 24 café orders were both app and tea. What is P(app and tea) for one uniformly selected order?
items.hint: This is a joint, not conditional, probability.
items.solution: P(app∩tea)=2/24=1/12 because the reference group is all 24 orders.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Two are drawn without replacement. What is P(red then red)?
items.hint: After drawing red, only 2 of the 4 remaining marbles are red.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: The same bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. What is P(blue then red) without replacement?
items.hint: After blue is removed, 3 of the remaining 4 marbles are red.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Suppose P(A)=0.30 and P(B | A)=0.40. What is P(A and B)?
items.hint: Multiply the marginal chance of A by the conditional chance of B after A.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

items.prompt: Why might P(A | B) and P(B | A) differ even though both use the same intersection?
items.hint: The two formulas share P(A∩B) but have different denominators.
items.solution: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) and P(B|A)=P(A∩B)/P(A). Different conditioning-group sizes can produce different values.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

options.label: B
options.text: The events must be mutually exclusive.

options.label: C
options.text: One of the probabilities has to be greater than 1.

options.label: D
options.text: The conditioning groups B and A have different probabilities.

items.prompt: When P(B)=0, which statement about P(A | B) is correct?
items.hint: The conditional rule divides by P(B).
items.solution: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B) requires P(B)>0; dividing by zero is undefined.
items.provenance: Maple Hill School original public-safe teaching practice, November 2026

options.label: A
options.text: It is undefined by the conditional probability formula.
